Random Generation from the Modified Half-Normal Distribution

Source: R/rmhn.R
rmhn.Rd

Draws random variates from the Modified Half-Normal (MHN) distribution with parameters alpha, beta, and gamma.

Usage

rmhn(n, alpha = 1, beta = 1, gamma = 0, method = c("auto", "rtdr", "sun"))

Arguments

n

Number of variates to draw: a non-negative number no larger than .Machine$integer.max, truncated to an integer, so that n = 0 returns numeric(0). Following the base R convention of rnorm() and rgamma(), if length(n) is not 1 the number required is taken to be length(n), so that a zero-length n also returns numeric(0); NULL is an error.

alpha

Shape parameter (\(\alpha > 0\)). Scalar or numeric vector. Default: 1.

beta

Rate-type parameter (\(\beta > 0\)), the coefficient of the Gaussian tail \(\exp(-\beta x^2)\); larger values pull mass toward zero. Scalar or numeric vector. Default: 1.

gamma

Tilt parameter (\(\gamma \in R\)), the coefficient of the exponential tilt \(\exp(\gamma x)\). Scalar or numeric vector. Default: 0.

method

Sampling algorithm. One of "auto" (default), "rtdr", or "sun". See Details.

Value

A numeric vector of length n. As in rnorm, an element whose parameters (after recycling to length n) are NA or NaN, or lie outside the parameter space (alpha or beta not positive and finite, or gamma not finite), is NaN, with a single warning "NAs produced", and draws no random numbers. A zero-length alpha, beta or gamma makes every element NA, with the same warning. The parameters must be numeric (double, integer or logical): a factor, a character string, a complex number, a list or NULL is an error. If a rejection sampler accepts none of 1000 proposals for an element (for a subnormal shape, none of 1000 draws of the proxy described under Subnormal shapes in Details, each of up to 1000 proposals), that element is NaN, and a single warning reports how many draws were affected; the acceptance rates of the samplers make this vanishingly unlikely. Where the distribution lies beyond the largest double precision number, and at some other extreme values, rmhn instead stops with an error for the whole call (see Details).

Details

The MHN density is $$f(x \mid \alpha, \beta, \gamma) = \frac{2 \beta^{\alpha/2} x^{\alpha-1} \exp(-\beta x^2 + \gamma x)}{\Psi[\alpha/2, \gamma/\sqrt{\beta}]} \quad (x > 0)$$ where \(\Psi[a, z] = \sum_{n \ge 0} \Gamma(a + n/2) z^n / n!\) is the Fox-Wright function \({}_1\Psi_1[(a, 1/2); (1, 0); z]\). rmhn does not evaluate \(\Psi\); the rejection-sampling kernels cancel it out. The one exception is the weight of the origin, \(1 / (1 + w)\), that it draws for a subnormal shape (see Subnormal shapes below).

The default parameters alpha = 1, beta = 1, gamma = 0 correspond to the half-normal distribution \(\mathrm{HN}(1/\sqrt{2})\).

Choice of sampler

Two closed-form special cases are taken first, whatever method: a negligible tilt, \(|\gamma|/\sqrt{\beta}\) within sqrt(.Machine$double.eps) of 0, is drawn as the square root of a Gamma variate, and a shape \(\alpha\) within sqrt(.Machine$double.eps) of 1 from a truncated normal. Both are exact samplers of their special-case law, which next to \(\gamma = 0\) or \(\alpha = 1\) is within a total variation distance of \(8.6 \times 10^{-9}\) of the law requested. The one exception is a negligible tilt above \(\alpha = 2^{60}\), which is drawn by the Normal proposal of Sun et al. (2023) Algorithm 1 centred at the mode, or by RTDR under method = "rtdr" (Sun et al. state Algorithm 1 for \(\gamma > 0\); centred at the mode, its Normal envelope holds for either sign). Otherwise method selects the rejection sampler:

  • "auto" (default): the faster of the provably correct samplers, as measured by timing them against each other. For \(\alpha < 1\) and \(\gamma > 0\) it uses RTDR. Otherwise it chooses between Sun et al. Algorithm 1 (\(\gamma > 0\)) or Algorithm 3 (\(\gamma < 0\)) and RTDR by the shape, the tilt \(\gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\) and the number of variates per setup (see Vector parameters and setups); Section 7 of vignette("theory", package = "mhn") gives the decision tree. The choice changes the speed and the stream of draws (see Reproducibility), not the law drawn.

  • "rtdr": the Relaxed Transformed Density Rejection method of Gao & Wang (2025). Gao & Wang bound its acceptance probability below by \(1/e \approx 0.368\) for every parameter value, provided the contact points of the envelope lie in the band of their Eq. (7); the search for them does not always reach that band, and the acceptance measured stays above the bound there too. Where RTDR cannot place a law of tiny shape under a strong negative tilt, Sun et al. Algorithm 3 is used instead (see Limits of double precision). Note: Gao & Wang (2025) use the parameterization \((\lambda, \alpha, \beta)\) with density proportional to \(x^{\lambda - 1} \exp(-\alpha x^2 - \beta x)\); the mapping to the Sun et al. parameterization used here is \(\lambda \leftrightarrow \alpha\), \(\alpha \leftrightarrow \beta\), \(\beta \leftrightarrow -\gamma\) (sign flip on the linear term).

  • "sun": the algorithms of Sun et al. (2023): Algorithm 1 for \(\gamma > 0\) and \(\alpha > 1\), and Algorithm 3 for \(\gamma < 0\), up to \(\alpha = 2^{59}\), beyond which the call stops with an error (see Limits of double precision). The combination \(\alpha < 1\) with \(\gamma > 0\) is unsupported: unless a special case answers it first, the call stops with the error Sun method not available for alpha<1 and gamma>0; use method="rtdr".

Vector parameters and setups

Vector parameters are recycled to length n following standard R rules: only the first n elements of each parameter are used, and any further elements are silently ignored, matching the convention of rnorm.

The setup of the chosen sampler is built once for each run of equal consecutive \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\) triples. Short parameter vectors repeat their triples after a period, the least common multiple of the lengths of alpha, beta and gamma; when that period is at most 256 draws and they are recycled over at least four such periods, a setup is kept for each position within the period. So passing parameters grouped by triple, or as short recycled vectors, is faster than calling rmhn inside an R loop, and a long run of one triple is drawn fastest by its own scalar call.

The number of variates per setup, from which method = "auto" chooses its sampler, and which therefore changes the draws for a fixed seed, is n for scalar parameters, and n divided by the period, rounded down, where a setup is kept for each position within the period. Otherwise it is 1: parameters given as vectors of length n count one per setup, as in a Gibbs sampler, even when equal triples are grouped into runs, and such a call draws what the loop of single draws would. Grouping saves setups but does not change this number, and so not the choice of sampler.

Reproducibility

Under one seed, method = "rtdr" and method = "sun" draw one stream whatever n: the first k draws of rmhn(n, ...) are those of rmhn(k, ...), and draws split over several calls are those of one call. The default method does not keep this, as it chooses its sampler from the number of variates per setup (see above): rmhn(4, 5, 1, 2) and the first four draws of rmhn(100, 5, 1, 2) come from different samplers. Its stream therefore changes with n, with how the parameters are arranged, and with a version of the package that moves a threshold, although the law drawn does not. Where the draws must not depend on n, as when a pilot run is compared with the main one, set method = "rtdr" or method = "sun".

Limits of double precision

Double precision limits which laws can be sampled, and how finely. Every sampler draws from the exact law and rounds the draw to double precision, and a draw below the smallest positive double is returned as 0. A rounding error that would shift every draw alike is kept to a few times \(10^{-7}\) of a standard deviation. For this reason the square-root-Gamma closed form is used only up to \(\alpha = 2^{60}\), and Sun et al. Algorithm 3 only up to \(\alpha = 2^{59}\) (about \(5.8 \times 10^{17}\)). Above \(\alpha = 2^{59}\) a negative tilt that is not negligible is drawn by RTDR under the default method, while method = "sun" stops with an error; a positive tilt is drawn by Algorithm 1 under both.

The RTDR sampler stops with an error for the whole call once the standard deviation is no larger than the spacing of the double precision numbers at the mode, so that its draws could take only a few distinct values: from \(\gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\) of about \(9 \times 10^{15}\) (\(2^{53}\) at \(\beta = 1\)), and, for \(\gamma \le 0\), from \(\alpha\) between \(2^{103}\) and \(2^{106}\) (\(1.0 \times 10^{31}\) to \(8.1 \times 10^{31}\)), depending on the tilt and on where the mode falls between two powers of two. There the law is normal to far below double precision, with mean \(m\) = mhn_mode(alpha, beta, gamma) and variance \(1/((\alpha - 1)/m^2 + 2\beta)\), and can be drawn from directly, as the error message suggests. Sun et al. Algorithm 1, which the default method uses for such laws with \(\gamma > 0\) and \(\alpha > 1\), and the truncated normal of \(\alpha \approx 1\) do not stop there: their draws are placed at the mode to within a few units in the last place, so that they take only a few distinct values near it.

RTDR cannot place the law in three cases, all under a negative tilt: where \(-\gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\) passes the largest double; for \(\alpha \le 1\), where \(\alpha\) is below about \(2.5 \times 10^{-324}\) times \(-\gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\), which needs \(\alpha\) below \(4.4 \times 10^{-16}\), and almost all the mass of \(X\) lies below the smallest positive double; and for a shape of a few, where \(-\gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\) comes within a small factor of the largest double. In the second case, and in the first for \(\alpha < 10^{-15}\), method = "rtdr" draws from Algorithm 3, which samples the law exactly there, except for a subnormal shape, which is drawn as described under Subnormal shapes; otherwise it stops with an error that names the Gamma distribution with shape \(\alpha\) and rate \(-\gamma\), which the law is to double precision. The default method uses Algorithm 3 in all three cases, except where \(-\gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\) passes the largest double at a shape above \(2^{59}\); there it stops as RTDR does. Where the distribution lies beyond the largest double precision number, no draw can represent it, and every sampler, the closed forms included, stops with an error.

Subnormal shapes

A subnormal shape, below the smallest normal double \(2.2 \times 10^{-308}\), is drawn as the mixture its law is (see the Details of dmhn): 0 with probability \(1 / (1 + w)\), the probability of a value below the smallest positive double, and otherwise from the peak, through a proxy: the law of the shape \(2^{-60}\) above \(\sqrt{\beta} x = 1\), drawn by the sampler method selects for that shape. The choice between 0 and the peak compares one uniform variate with \(1 / (1 + w)\), and so has the resolution of the generator, \(2^{-32}\) for R's default. Where \(1 / (1 + w)\) is 1 in double precision, below a tilt of about 52 (53 at the smallest shapes), every draw is 0 and uses no random number; a shape from \(2^{-1022}\) up is drawn by the samplers above, which use random numbers there too, so that the stream after the draws moves as the shape crosses \(2^{-1022}\) although every draw is 0 on either side. A refusal names the shape asked for.

The algorithms, the timings behind the choice of method = "auto", and the handling of extreme parameters are described in vignette("theory", package = "mhn") (Section 7 and Appendix A).

References

Sun, J., Kong, M., & Pal, S. (2023). The Modified-Half-Normal distribution: Properties and an efficient sampling scheme. Communications in Statistics - Theory and Methods, 52(5), 1591–1613. doi:10.1080/03610926.2021.1934700

Gao, F., & Wang, H.-B. (2025). Generating modified-half-normal random variates by a relaxed transformed density rejection method. Communications in Statistics - Simulation and Computation, 1–25. Advance online publication. doi:10.1080/03610918.2025.2524551

Robert, C. P. (1995). Simulation of truncated normal variables. Statistics and Computing, 5(2), 121–125. doi:10.1007/BF00143942

See also

dmhn, mhn_mean, mhn_var

Examples

set.seed(1)
rmhn(10, alpha = 2, beta = 1, gamma = 0.5)
#>  [1] 0.4882149 1.7209460 0.2702322 0.5039321 1.0199839 0.8549756 0.5065696
#>  [8] 1.1410072 0.7866116 1.0854880

# Vector parameters are recycled to length n.
set.seed(1)
rmhn(5, alpha = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))
#> [1] 0.4429697 0.7989284 0.5821857 1.4320656 2.2998471
